lead: Tacheometry measures a distance from an angle, not from a chain. A staff or bar of known length stands at the far station; the theodolite measures the small angle it subtends, and that angle fixes the horizontal distance and the elevation in the same sighting. The method is fast enough for contouring and for detail across a river, a railway line or a crowded Chennai street where a tape cannot go. Stadia, subtense and tangential are three ways to get the known length and the angle.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for vertical angles, Chapter 4.1 for the instrument, Unit 3 for reduced levels, and Unit 1 for the idea of a subtended angle and electronic distance measurement.

blocks.text: A length held at the far station subtends an angle at the instrument. For a small angle, the length equals distance times angle in radians, so distance is length divided by angle. Tacheometry uses this one relation to avoid chaining. A graduated staff is held at the staff station, and the telescope reads the length between two marks; that length is the staff intercept s, in metres.

The stadia system adds two horizontal hairs to the telescope, one above and one below the centre hair. The separation of these outer hairs is the stadia interval i, in metres at the diaphragm. With f the focal length of the object glass and d the distance from the object glass to the vertical axis, the lens geometry gives D = K s + C. K = f/i is the stadia constant, usually 100. C = f + d is the additive constant, usually between 0 and 0.3 m. An anallatic lens makes C zero, so the field reduction is only D = 100 s.

blocks.where: D is the horizontal distance from the instrument axis to the staff, in metres; K = f/i is the stadia constant; s is the staff intercept, in metres; C = f + d is the additive constant, in metres.

items: Fixed hairs: the outer hairs are permanent, and K and C are instrument constants.
Movable hairs: one hair is moved until the intercept is a round number; the stadia constant is then read from a scale.

blocks.text: When the line of sight is inclined at a vertical angle θ above the horizontal, the staff is still held vertical. The intercept s on the staff is not perpendicular to the line of sight. Its component perpendicular to the sight is s cos θ. The inclined distance from the instrument to the staff is therefore K(s cos θ) + C. Projecting that distance on the horizontal and vertical gives two equations.
D = K s cos²θ + C cosθ
blocks.where: D is horizontal distance in metres; θ is the vertical angle; s is the staff intercept on a vertical staff, in metres; K and C are the stadia constants.

blocks.text: V = K s sinθ cosθ + C sinθ
blocks.where: V is the vertical component from the instrument axis to the mid hair, in metres, positive upward; other symbols as above.

blocks.text: The cos²θ is the common mistake. The first cosθ turns the vertical staff intercept into a length perpendicular to the sight; the second cosθ turns the inclined distance into a horizontal distance. If the staff is held normal to the line of sight, s is already perpendicular, so D = (K s + C) cosθ and V = (K s + C) sinθ. The normal staff gets one cosθ only. Holding a staff normal is awkward on a sloping sight, so the vertical staff is standard.

The method is used for contouring and for detail that cannot be chained: across a river, a railway yard, or a crowded street. One sighting gives both D and V, and the reduced level follows with the mid-hair reading.

A subtense bar is a horizontal bar of fixed length s, commonly 2.000 m, set at the far station. The theodolite at the instrument station measures the whole angle θ between the two ends of the bar. The triangle gives D = s / (2 tan(θ/2)). For small θ, tan(θ/2) ≈ θ/2, so D ≈ s/θ, with θ in radians. The angle is the whole angle subtended by the bar, not half. A two-instrument version puts a short base at the instrument station; two theodolites at its ends sight the same distant target, and the triangle gives the distance.

The tangential method uses two vertical angles to two targets on the same vertical line. Let α₁ be the angle to the upper target, α₂ to the lower, and s the vertical distance between the targets. The horizontal distance is D = s / (tan α₁ − tan α₂). Use algebraic signs when one angle is a depression. The method suits a long sight where the staff reading is unreliable because of refraction or because the target is on a boat or a bridge.

blocks.where: D is horizontal distance in metres; s is the vertical separation of the two targets in metres; α₁ and α₂ are the vertical angles to the upper and lower targets, with signs.

blocks.text: A total station measures D directly by EDM, so tacheometry is now a check or a fallback. See Unit 5 for that hardware.

figure.caption: The staff intercept 1.250 m and vertical angle 8°12′ give D = 122.46 m and V = 17.65 m, so the staff station RL is 118.300 m. Notice the same intercept feeds both the horizontal and vertical branches.

spec.title: One sighting, two answers
spec.aria: Flowchart from reading the staff intercept, through the stadia constants, to the horizontal distance and the vertical component, and finally to the reduced level of the staff station.

examples.question: A tacheometer with K = 100 and C = 0 sights a staff held vertically. The intercept between the top and bottom hairs is 1.250 m and the vertical angle is 8°12′. The mid hair reads 1.850 m and the reduced level of the instrument axis is 102.500 m. Find D, V and the reduced level of the staff station. Take cos 8°12′ = 0.98978 and sin 8°12′ = 0.14263.
steps: Convert the vertical angle: θ = 8°12′ = 8 + 12/60 = 8.2°. The given values are cos θ = 0.98978 and sin θ = 0.14263.
Write the data with units: K = 100, C = 0, s = 1.250 m, mid-hair reading = 1.850 m, instrument-axis RL = 102.500 m.
Horizontal distance: D = K s cos²θ + C cosθ = 100 × 1.250 × 0.98978² + 0. Here 0.98978² = 0.97966, so D = 125 × 0.97966 = 122.46 m.
Vertical component: V = K s sinθ cosθ + C sinθ = 100 × 1.250 × 0.14263 × 0.98978 + 0 = 125 × 0.14117 = 17.65 m.
Reduced level of the staff station: RL = instrument-axis RL + V − mid reading = 102.500 + 17.65 − 1.850 = 118.300 m.
examples.answer: D = 122.46 m, V = 17.65 m, and the reduced level of the staff station is 118.300 m.
examples.check:
import math
K = 100.0
C = 0.0
s = 1.250
theta = math.radians(8 + 12/60)
mid = 1.850
rl_axis = 102.500
D = K*s*math.cos(theta)**2 + C*math.cos(theta)
V = K*s*math.sin(theta)*math.cos(theta) + C*math.sin(theta)
rl = rl_axis + V - mid
print(round(D, 2))
print(round(V, 2))
print(round(rl, 3))

traps: Using D = 100 s on an inclined sight and dropping the cos²θ factor. The vertical staff intercept must first be made perpendicular to the sight, then projected horizontally.
In the subtense method the angle must be in radians for D ≈ s/θ, and θ is the whole angle subtended by the bar, not half of it.
Mixing the vertical-staff and normal-staff formulas. A vertical staff on an inclined sight gives K s cos²θ + C cosθ; a normal staff gives (K s + C) cosθ, with one cosθ only.
Treating C as an angle or as a large correction. C is a length in metres, usually 0 to 0.3 m, and it becomes zero only with an anallatic lens.
In the tangential method, s is the vertical separation of the two targets, not a staff intercept, and the two vertical angles must carry their correct signs.

quiz.q: Define staff intercept in stadia tacheometry.
quiz.a: The staff intercept is the distance on the staff, in metres, between the top and bottom stadia hairs as read through the telescope.

quiz.q: Why does a vertical staff on an inclined sight give a cos²θ term in the horizontal distance?
quiz.a: The staff intercept is inclined to the line of sight, so its perpendicular component is s cosθ. The inclined distance built from that component is then projected to the horizontal, giving a second cosθ. Hence D = K s cos²θ + C cosθ.

quiz.q: A tacheometer has K = 100 and C = 0. The staff is vertical, the intercept is 1.500 m and the vertical angle is 10°00′. Find D and V. Use cos 10° = 0.98481 and sin 10° = 0.17365.
A subtense bar 2.000 m long subtends a whole angle of 0°40′. Find the horizontal distance by the small-angle formula.
Why might a surveyor choose the tangential method instead of the stadia method for a long sight?
quiz.a: At a long sight the staff reading becomes unreliable because of refraction, poor illumination or an unsteady target. The tangential method uses two vertical angles to two targets with a known vertical separation, so it avoids depending on a fine staff reading.

quiz.q: What does an anallatic lens do to the tacheometric constants?
quiz.a: It changes the optical geometry so that the additive constant C becomes zero. The field reduction then reduces to D = K s, with K usually 100.

quiz.q: Give two field uses of tacheometry.
quiz.a: Contouring and filling in detail quickly; also measuring across a river, a railway line or a crowded street where chaining is not possible.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern total stations replace the stadia hair by an EDM beam and compute D and V inside the instrument, so the old formulas survive as checks and as fallback when the reflector is lost. Subtense bars still appear in deformation monitoring and in tunnels where a target cannot be occupied. Search for 'stadia formula derivation', 'subtense bar accuracy' and 'tacheometric contouring' if you want the next layer.
